title: Full Functional Dependency
description: Understand full functional dependency using determinant minimality, closures, valid counterexamples and the link to 2NF, without confusing a data snapshot with a domain proof.
notes:
## Ask whether every determinant attribute is necessary

A functional dependency X determines Y means that any two valid relation rows agreeing on all attributes in X must also agree on Y. A full functional dependency adds a minimality requirement: Y depends on the whole determinant X, and no proper subset of X determines Y. The word full describes whether any determinant attribute can be removed without losing the dependency.

Consider a campus assessment relation with student_id, assessment_id and awarded_mark. If each student receives one recorded mark for each assessment, the pair student_id and assessment_id determines awarded_mark. The dependency is full when neither student_id alone nor assessment_id alone determines that mark. The student can take different assessments, and different students can receive different marks on one assessment.

## State the domain rule before examining a sample

Functional dependencies describe allowed states, not merely coincidences in one displayed table. A sample in which every student has taken only one assessment might make student_id appear to determine awarded_mark. The domain may still permit that student to take another assessment and receive a different mark. The visible agreement is therefore insufficient to establish the dependency as a rule.

Write the intended invariant in ordinary language: one current awarded mark belongs to one student-assessment pair. Also state whether attempts, components or grading revisions are separate facts. If multiple attempts can coexist, the pair may no longer determine a unique mark without an attempt identity or a defined current-result rule. Full-dependency analysis must use the actual record meaning rather than a convenient column list.

## Separate dependency from full dependency

If student_id alone determines student_name, then the larger pair student_id and assessment_id also determines student_name. Adding an attribute to a determinant does not invalidate a dependency that already holds. However, the larger dependency is not full because assessment_id is unnecessary. It is a partial dependency relative to that composite determinant.

This distinction explains why a statement can be a true functional dependency yet fail the full-dependency test. The existence question asks whether agreeing on X forces agreement on Y. The minimality question asks whether every attribute in X is needed. Evaluate them in that order, because a dependency that does not hold cannot become full simply because both columns seem important to the application.

## Use closures to reason systematically

Attribute closure collects everything implied by a chosen determinant under a specified dependency set. To test X determines Y, compute the closure of X and check whether it contains Y. To test fullness, inspect whether any proper subset of X also has a closure containing Y. For a two-attribute determinant, the individual singleton closures are the first cases to examine.

For larger finite determinants, testing every single-attribute removal from X is sufficient for this minimality check: if any smaller proper subset determined Y, an appropriate one-attribute-removed superset would determine Y as well. This follows from augmentation of functional dependencies. Do not test only one convenient subset and assume that the remaining determinant attributes are necessary too.

## Work through a campus relation

Let the relation contain Student, Assessment, StudentName, AssessmentTitle and Mark. Suppose the intended dependencies are Student determines StudentName, Assessment determines AssessmentTitle, and Student plus Assessment determines Mark. The pair's closure reaches every attribute, so it is a candidate key if neither singleton reaches the whole relation. Those dependencies summarize different responsibilities within the same wide table.

Student plus Assessment determines StudentName, but not fully: Student already determines the name. The analogous dependency to AssessmentTitle is also partial. The dependency to Mark is full under the stated set because neither Student nor Assessment alone reaches Mark. The conclusion depends on these domain constraints; adding a new rule such as every assessment awarding one fixed mark could change the analysis.

| Determinant | Dependent | Full under the stated rules? |
|---|---|---|
| Student, Assessment | Mark | Yes |
| Student, Assessment | StudentName | No: Student suffices |
| Student, Assessment | AssessmentTitle | No: Assessment suffices |

The table is a dependency diagram in tabular form, not evidence from a production database. Its purpose is to show which determinant components matter. A reader should be able to explain why removing Student loses the mark dependency and why removing Assessment also loses it, while removing Assessment does not lose the student-name dependency.

## Use counterexamples to challenge minimality

To show Student does not determine Mark, construct two allowed rows for one student on different assessments with different marks. To show Assessment does not determine Mark, construct two allowed rows for different students on the same assessment with different marks. These are different counterexamples because they challenge different proper subsets of the pair.

The examples must be allowed by the domain. If the application permits only one assessment per student, the first counterexample is invalid and the proposed dependency analysis needs revision. A useful exercise is to describe the business permission before writing the counterexample rows. That prevents a purely visual table manipulation from contradicting the requirements the dependencies are supposed to formalize.

## Do not confuse key size with fullness

A composite key does not automatically make every dependency from it full. StudentName remains dependent on only Student even when the table's chosen primary key is Student plus Assessment. Conversely, a full dependency can involve an arbitrary determinant, not only the primary key. The formal definition concerns necessity within X; normalization applies that reasoning to particular keys and attributes.

A single-attribute determinant has no nonempty proper subset, but the empty set is still relevant in the formal definition. A dependent that is constant throughout all permitted states can be determined by the empty set. Avoid the absolute shortcut that every dependency from one attribute is automatically full under every possible dependency system. Introductory examples often omit constants, but a careful definition explains the assumption.

## Relate the idea to second normal form

Second normal form requires first normal form and no partial dependency of a nonprime attribute on any candidate key. A nonprime attribute belongs to no candidate key. Full-dependency analysis helps identify whether a nonprime attribute needs the whole composite key or is actually determined by only one component. It is therefore one tool in evaluating 2NF, rather than a complete definition of good design.

Check every candidate key, not only the key designated PRIMARY KEY in the implementation. A table can have alternate candidate keys that reveal a partial dependency missed by a primary-key-only review. Also avoid applying the nonprime restriction loosely: prime attributes have a particular role in normalization definitions, and replacing that distinction with all columns can produce an incorrect verdict.

## Decompose responsibilities without losing relationships

In the campus example, separate Students(Student, StudentName), Assessments(Assessment, AssessmentTitle), and Results(Student, Assessment, Mark). Each descriptive attribute then lives with its determinant, while the result relation keeps the student-assessment relationship. This avoids repeating a student's name on every result and avoids requiring an assessment result just to store a new assessment title.

A decomposition should be checked for lossless reconstruction and the preservation of relevant dependencies, not merely admired because the tables are smaller. The relationship keys must remain explicit. Renaming or deleting a key component to simplify an example can lose the very fact whose mark requires both identities. Continue with [2NF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/2nf) and [functional dependencies](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/functional-dependency) for the associated design checks.

## Use SQL as a detector, not a proof of the rule

A grouped query can find a current counterexample to an asserted dependency. For example, more than one distinct known mark for the same determinant in a snapshot contradicts a simple nonnull single-mark rule. Absence of such a group does not prove that every future valid state obeys the rule. Constraints and domain analysis establish permitted states; a current data scan only observes one state.

```sql
SELECT student_id, COUNT(DISTINCT awarded_mark) AS known_marks
FROM result_snapshot
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT awarded_mark) > 1;
```

This diagnostic can refute Student determines Mark when it finds different known marks for a student. It cannot decide the whole full-dependency question on its own, and COUNT DISTINCT has its own null behavior. The exercises therefore emphasize dependency reasoning and allowed counterexamples. A successful SQL scan should never be reported as a mathematical proof of the application invariant.

questions.question_text: Under the stated campus rules, why is Student,Assessment determines Mark full?
options: The pair is printed first
The pair determines Mark, and neither single identity does
Mark is numeric
The sample contains exactly one row
questions.explanation: Both determinant components are necessary under the specified permitted-state rules.

questions.question_text: Two allowed rows have the same Assessment but different Mark values. What does this refute?
options: The pair necessarily determines Mark
Assessment alone determines Mark
Student alone determines Mark
Every possible dependency in the relation
questions.explanation: It refutes that singleton dependency only. Establishing fullness also requires the pair dependency and the other subset check.

questions.question_text: For a full functional dependency to exist on a composite key X = {A, B}, what must be true?
options: Both A -> Y and B -> Y must hold individually
X -> Y must hold, AND neither A alone nor B alone may determine Y
Y must be part of the key itself
A and B must both be foreign keys
questions.explanation: Full functional dependency requires the whole composite determinant, with no proper subset (here, A alone or B alone) sufficient to determine Y on its own.

questions.question_text: Why must a careful fullness definition consider the empty set even for a singleton determinant?
options: The empty set contains all key attributes
A dependent fixed by the domain can be determined by the empty set
Every singleton determinant is necessarily composite
Constants can never appear in relations
questions.explanation: Fullness rules out every proper determining subset. The familiar singleton shortcut assumes no empty-set dependency on the dependent.

questions.question_text: Under the campus rules, which dependency from Student,Assessment is partial?
options: The dependency to Mark when neither singleton determines it
The dependency to AssessmentTitle, because Assessment alone suffices
Every dependency from any pair
Only dependencies to numeric columns
questions.explanation: The student component is unnecessary for the assessment title.

questions.question_text: A table has key {OrderID, ProductID} and an attribute ShipDate that is the same for every ProductID within a given OrderID (the whole order ships together). Is ShipDate fully dependent on {OrderID, ProductID}?
options: Yes, because it depends on the composite key
No — since ShipDate is determined by OrderID alone (a proper subset), it is only partially dependent, not fully dependent, on the composite key
Yes, because ShipDate is a date type
No, because ShipDate cannot be functionally dependent on anything
questions.explanation: OrderID alone fixes ShipDate, so ProductID is unnecessary in that determinant. This is analogous to an assessment title determined by Assessment alone.

questions.question_text: What is the relevant 2NF restriction after first normal form?
options: Every selected primary-key column must be numeric
No nonprime attribute has a partial dependency on any candidate key
Every dependent must be in every key
Only the declared primary key is examined
questions.explanation: Nonprime means belonging to no candidate key, and alternate candidate keys must also be considered.

questions.question_text: Assume StudentID determines StudentName. Is {StudentID, CourseID} -> StudentName a full functional dependency?
options: Yes, because StudentID is part of the composite key
No — StudentID alone already determines StudentName, so it is a partial dependency, not a full one
Yes, because CourseID is required to determine StudentName
There is not enough information to decide
questions.explanation: Since StudentID by itself (a proper subset of the composite key) determines StudentName, the dependency is partial, not full — CourseID adds nothing to the determination.

questions.question_text: What additional condition makes X determines Y full?
options: No proper subset of X determines Y
X must be a primary key name
Y must be numeric
The table must have one row
questions.explanation: Fullness is minimality of the determinant.

questions.question_text: Does Student determine StudentName imply Student,Assessment determines StudentName?
options: No, adding attributes invalidates dependencies
Yes, but that larger dependency is partial
Only when names are unique
Only in SQL tables
questions.explanation: The added determinant attribute is unnecessary.

questions.question_text: Which counterexample challenges Student determines Mark?
options: Two students with the same mark
One student with one mark
One student with different marks on two allowed assessments
Two different names only
questions.explanation: Equal determinant values with different dependents refute the dependency.

questions.question_text: Which counterexample challenges Assessment determines Mark?
options: Two assessments with different titles
One result row
A student with a repeated name
Different students with different marks on the same assessment
questions.explanation: The assessment agrees while the mark differs.

questions.question_text: What establishes a dependency as a domain rule?
options: Constraints on all permitted states
One accidental sample pattern
The column position
The query alias
questions.explanation: A snapshot alone is not a general proof.

questions.question_text: How can closure test X determines Y?
options: Count the rows in X
Check whether Y is contained in X closure
Sort Y alphabetically
Require X to contain every column initially
questions.explanation: Closure collects implied attributes.

questions.question_text: For a larger determinant, what removals suffice to test minimality?
options: Only the first removal
Only the largest-valued attribute
Every single-attribute removal
No removals if a primary key exists
questions.explanation: Any determining smaller subset would imply a determining one-removal superset.

questions.question_text: What happens if multiple attempts coexist under one student-assessment pair?
options: The pair necessarily still determines every mark
All marks become equal
The dependency is automatically full
An attempt identity or current-result rule may be needed
questions.explanation: The fact grain must reflect permitted repeated attempts.

questions.question_text: Which keys matter when checking 2NF partial dependencies?
options: All candidate keys
Only the declared primary key
Only foreign keys
Only surrogate keys
questions.explanation: Alternate candidate keys can reveal partial dependencies.

questions.question_text: What is a nonprime attribute?
options: Any numeric attribute
An attribute belonging to no candidate key
Every foreign key
Only the last column
questions.explanation: 2NF uses this formal distinction.

questions.question_text: Can a data scan prove a dependency for every future valid state?
options: Yes, if the table is large
Yes, with ORDER BY
No
Only with COUNT DISTINCT
questions.explanation: Current observations do not establish all allowed states.

questions.question_text: What must a proposed decomposition preserve?
options: Only the original column order
Only the original row count in one sample
Every repeated name
A lossless relationship and relevant dependency guarantees
questions.explanation: Smaller tables alone do not establish design correctness.

coding_not_applicable: The learning objective is proof of determinant minimality over permitted states. SQL scans can expose a present counterexample but cannot prove universal functional dependencies. The notes provide two explicit counterexample-construction exercises and a carefully bounded SQL diagnostic; query-judged exercises would misrepresent the proof requirement.

original_questions.question_text: Why is {StudentID, CourseID} -> EnrollmentDate classified as a FULL functional dependency?
options: Because EnrollmentDate is a date data type
Because neither StudentID alone nor CourseID alone determines EnrollmentDate — the entire composite key is required
Because EnrollmentDate is part of the primary key
Because CourseID alone already determines EnrollmentDate
original_questions.explanation: Full functional dependency means no proper subset of the composite key determines the attribute; here both StudentID alone and CourseID alone fail to pin down EnrollmentDate, only the pair does.

original_questions.question_text: In the sample data, C1 (Database Systems) has three different EnrollmentDate values (2026-01-10, 2026-01-11, 2026-01-12) across S1, S2, and S3. What does this prove?
options: That CourseID alone determines EnrollmentDate
That CourseID alone does NOT determine EnrollmentDate, ruling out CourseID as a sufficient determinant by itself
That EnrollmentDate is not a valid attribute
That StudentID alone determines EnrollmentDate
original_questions.explanation: If the same CourseID value corresponds to different EnrollmentDate values across rows, CourseID alone cannot be a determinant of EnrollmentDate — confirming the dependency needs the full composite key.

original_questions.question_text: For a full functional dependency to exist on a composite key X = {A, B}, what must be true?
options: Both A -> Y and B -> Y must hold individually
X -> Y must hold, AND neither A alone nor B alone may determine Y
Y must be part of the key itself
A and B must both be foreign keys
original_questions.explanation: Full functional dependency requires the whole composite determinant, with no proper subset (here, A alone or B alone) sufficient to determine Y on its own.

original_questions.question_text: Why is full functional dependency only a meaningful question when the key is composite (more than one attribute)?
options: Because single-attribute keys never have functional dependencies
Because with a single-attribute key there is no non-empty proper subset to compare against, so every dependency on it is trivially 'full'
Because composite keys are always artificial/surrogate
Because full functional dependency requires exactly two attributes in the key
original_questions.explanation: The 'full vs partial' distinction only makes sense when you can ask 'does some smaller subset of the key already determine this?' — a single-attribute key has no smaller non-empty subset to test.

original_questions.question_text: Which attribute in the running example is NOT fully dependent on {StudentID, CourseID} (i.e., is only partially dependent)?
options: EnrollmentDate
CourseName, since CourseID alone already determines it
There are no partially dependent attributes in this table
StudentID itself
original_questions.explanation: CourseName depends on CourseID alone, a proper subset of the composite key — that's a partial dependency (21.7), the opposite of full functional dependency.

original_questions.question_text: A table has key {OrderID, ProductID} and an attribute ShipDate that is the same for every ProductID within a given OrderID (the whole order ships together). Is ShipDate fully dependent on {OrderID, ProductID}?
options: Yes, because it depends on the composite key
No — since ShipDate is determined by OrderID alone (a proper subset), it is only partially dependent, not fully dependent, on the composite key
Yes, because ShipDate is a date type
No, because ShipDate cannot be functionally dependent on anything
original_questions.explanation: If OrderID alone already fixes ShipDate, the composite key is not fully necessary — this is a partial dependency, structurally identical to the CourseName situation in the running example.

original_questions.question_text: Why does full functional dependency matter for schema design, specifically for 2NF?
options: It has no connection to normal forms
2NF requires every non-key attribute to be fully functionally dependent on the whole key; attributes that are only partially dependent must be moved to a different relation
Full functional dependency is only relevant to BCNF
It determines whether a table needs a foreign key
original_questions.explanation: 2NF is defined exactly in terms of full functional dependency — any attribute that is only partially dependent on the key violates 2NF and must be relocated.

original_questions.question_text: Is {StudentID, CourseID} -> StudentName a full functional dependency?
options: Yes, because StudentID is part of the composite key
No — StudentID alone already determines StudentName, so it is a partial dependency, not a full one
Yes, because CourseID is required to determine StudentName
There is not enough information to decide
original_questions.explanation: Since StudentID by itself (a proper subset of the composite key) determines StudentName, the dependency is partial, not full — CourseID adds nothing to the determination.
